span.label: whether working-memory-related hippocampal activity patterns during a word list predict long-term encoding, and explain the primacy effect
span.quote: Here, we used two complimentary approaches to investigate whether WM-related activity patterns occur also during LTM encoding of sequentially presented items and whether they are related to the primacy effect, i.e., improved LTM encoding of items presented at the beginning of the list.

span.label: which form of working memory supports the items at the start of a list
span.quote: However, it is still an open question which forms of WM support memory for these items.

span.label: shows hippocampal deactivation at the first list position predicts that the item will be forgotten, linking a working-memory signature to long-term encoding failure
span.quote: However, deactivations of the hippocampus as previously observed during WM maintenance of individual items predicts failure of LTM encoding.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Our present findings demonstrate that hippocampus-independent WM at early list-positions is not beneficial for LTM and results in subsequent forgetting.

span.label: working memory-long-term memory interaction in the hippocampus
span.quote: Here, we used two complimentary approaches to investigate whether WM-related activity patterns occur also during LTM encoding of sequentially presented items and whether they are related to the primacy effect, i.e., improved LTM encoding of items presented at the beginning of the list.

span.label: fmri
span.quote: Intracranial electroencephalogram in epilepsy patients and functional MRI in healthy subjects were recorded during a word-list learning task.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: Our present findings demonstrate that hippocampus-independent WM at early list-positions is not beneficial for LTM and results in subsequent forgetting.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: Recruitment of hippocampus-dependent WM at early list positions thus actually supports LTM formation.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: Based on the model of Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) , we suggest that items later in the list are not rehearsed as much as the items earlier in the list (explaining the primacy effect) and that later items interfere with previous words.

span.label: working memory is divided by neural signature: hippocampal activation for multiple items, deactivation for individual items
span.quote: A recent study showed that maintenance of multiple items was associated with hippocampal activation (hippocampus-dependent WM), while maintenance of individual items induced hippocampal deactivations (hippocampus-independent WM).

span.label: positive DC slopes in the iEEG are taken to correspond to BOLD deactivations, which is what lets the two datasets be read together
span.quote: These results are consistent with our iEEG findings because positive DC shifts likely correspond to deactivations

span.label: items at the start of a list are proposed to be rehearsed more, linking the primacy effect to working memory
span.quote: It has been proposed that the primacy effect is due to the fact that items at early list positions undergo more extensive rehearsal than items presented later ( Rundus, 1971 ; Brodie and Murdock, 1977 ). This idea suggests a link between LTM formation and rehearsal processes, which are attributed to working memory

span.label: successful early items are encoded in runs: encoding the first raises the conditional probability of encoding the second and third
span.quote: For the iEEG subjects, encoding success at the second position was indeed slightly higher if the first item was successfully encoded: While overall probability for LTM encoding at the second list position was 0.35, it increased to 0.51 if only trials where the first word was already successfully encoded were taken into account (conditional probability of encoding the second item given that the first item was encoded).

span.label: only the hemisphere contralateral to the seizure focus was analysed, in patients with confirmed unilateral sclerosis
span.quote: Only data from the hemisphere contralateral to the seizure onset zone were considered for analysis.

span.label: No behavioural measure of working-memory performance was collected, so it is unknown which items were actually held in WM.
span.quote: It should be noted that there is no behavioral monitoring of WM performance in the current experiment.

span.label: The link between the observed activity and actual long-term memory consequences of WM performance cannot be established.
span.quote: Therefore, we do not know for sure how LTM is actually affected by the WM performance for specific items, i.e., it is unknown which items are actually maintained in WM.

span.label: The proposed link to persistent activity recorded in vitro is acknowledged as speculative.
span.quote: It should be noted, though, that this analogy between electrophysiological data in vitro and the neural patterns during WM maintenance must remain speculative at the current stage.

span.label: Position-specific subsequent-memory analyses were statistically underpowered.
span.quote: Possibly, this lack of an effect is related to the reduced statistical power for position-specific analyses of subsequent memory effects.

span.label: the two populations differ in recall performance despite a shorter recall phase for the fMRI group
span.quote: Despite this shorter recall phase, the number of words recalled by the fMRI subjects was significantly higher than the number of words recalled by the patients

span.label: the paradigms differ between the two versions in presentation time, interstimulus interval, block count and recall duration
span.quote: In the fMRI version ( Fig. 1 C ), 40 blocks (also with 12 words in each block) were presented. Stimuli were presented for 1000 ms using goggles (which required longer presentation times). Interstimulus intervals ranged from 1.5 s to 1.9 s (mean 1.7 s). The duration of the recall phase was 60 s. This period was thus 30 s shorter than for the iEEG subjects to limit the overall length of the paradigm.

span.label: patients showed both primacy and recency; the fMRI subjects showed no recency at all
span.quote: Post hoc comparisons showed that recognition performance of the first three items was superior to recognition performance of items at all other positions (primacy effect). No recency effects at the end of the list became apparent.

span.label: the whole-brain effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and are reported at the cluster level instead
span.quote: These effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, but did have a large extension of 60 voxels for the serial position contrast of subsequently forgotten words and even 204 voxels for the serial position contrast of subsequently remembered items. Because of this large extension, activations were significant at the cluster level ( p < 0.05 for subsequently forgotten items and p < 0.001 for subsequently remembered items).

span.quote: For subsequently forgotten items, however, we found a trend for an effect of position ( F (2,36) = 2.943; p = 0.070; ε = 0.922) and for a linear effect of position ( F (1,18) = 4.249; p = 0.054), again consistent with our iEEG data.

span.quote: For the right hippocampus, a three-way ANOVA did not reveal an effect of, or interaction with, the factor position (all p > 0.3), but a significant main effect of memory ( F (1,18) = 8.898; p < 0.01).

span.label: the required rote strategy is verified only by asking participants afterwards
span.quote: All subjects were required to use a rote strategy to memorize each word avoiding memory aids such as making rows, sentences, stories or pictures. In other words, this strategy only involved subvocal repetitions of the words. This was explained thoroughly to all subjects; during debriefing, all subjects assured not to have used any elaborate strategy.

span.label: serial position curves and the primacy effect, imported as the behavioural handle on a neural question
span.quote: It has been proposed that the primacy effect is due to the fact that items at early list positions undergo more extensive rehearsal than items presented later ( Rundus, 1971 ; Brodie and Murdock, 1977 ). This idea suggests a link between LTM formation and rehearsal processes, which are attributed to working memory

span.quote: A recent study showed that maintenance of multiple items was associated with hippocampal activation (hippocampus-dependent WM), while maintenance of individual items induced hippocampal deactivations (hippocampus-independent WM).

span.quote: For subsequently forgotten items, we observed a deactivation during presentation of the first item which was reduced during presentation of items presented later in the list

span.label: effects of position and LINEAR effects of position are distinguished explicitly, with the a priori assumption of the second stated: that if there are effects across positions, these should be linear
span.quote: In other words, effects of position tested the null-hypothesis that slopes of DC potentials (or BOLD responses, respectively) from a number of different positions are identical (i.e., if the first three positions entered the ANOVA, that there is no difference between positions 1, 2 and 3). In contrast, linear effects of positions tested the null-hypothesis that slopes of DC potentials (or BOLD responses, respectively) at consecutive positions do not show a consistent linear change (i.e., that they change in the positive direction for some subjects and in a negative direction for other subjects). In other words, the test for linear effects of position makes the a priori assumption that if there are effects across positions, these should be linear.

In contrast, linear effects of positions tested the null-hypothesis that slopes of DC potentials (or BOLD responses, respectively) at consecutive positions do not show a consistent linear change (i.e., that they change in the positive direction for some subjects and in a negative direction for other subjects). span.label: Early-list words that were later forgotten were accompanied by hippocampal deactivation signatures in both fMRI and intracranial EEG.
span.quote: Items at the beginning of the list which were subsequently forgotten were associated with negative blood oxygen level dependent responses and positive direct current slopes, corresponding to hippocampal deactivations, suggesting that they were not processed in hippocampus-dependent WM.

span.label: No such deactivation appeared for later list items or for items that were successfully remembered.
span.quote: These deactivations were absent for items later in the list and for subsequently remembered items.

span.label: A second, independent general linear model reproduced the effect: left-hippocampal negative BOLD for forgotten items at position one was absent at position seven.

span.label: The position effect was left-lateralised: the right hippocampus showed a main effect of subsequent memory but no position effect.

Recordings were performed at the Department of Epileptology, University of Bonn, Germany. All patients had bilateral hippocampal depth electrodes. No seizure occurred within 24 h before the experiment. Only data from the hemisphere contralateral to the seizure onset zone were considered for analysis.
